k202.text: A frog and a mosquito! Both lay their eggs in water, and both have young that look nothing like the adult. Are their life cycles the same?

k301a.text: A little cicada is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

k301b.text: Cicadas sing loudly, but they hide well. Look on the tree trunks!

k301r.text: You against the Buddies! Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

h501.text: Are you ready? Three! Two! One! Go!

k501.text: Round one! Are their life cycles the same? Show me your fingers!

k503.text: One! They both lay eggs in water, and both babies look nothing like their parents. So they are the same!

k504.text: Two! A frog is big and green, and a mosquito is tiny and buzzy. They are totally different!

k505.text: Two. I counted the stages on our board. The frog has three, but the mosquito has four.

k601m.text: But I found two things that are the same! How can their life cycles be different?

k602.text: Look closer. When we compare, we look for what is the same, and what is different.

k603.text: What is the same are similarities. What is different are differences.

k604b.text: Similarities are the things both life cycles have in common. Differences are the ways they are not the same.

k605.text: Momo found two real similarities. Both lay their eggs in water, and in both, the young do not look like the adult.

k606.text: But is there a difference? Let's count the stages.

k701.text: Be a raindrop! Shrink down. Quietly.

k702.text: You fall into the garden pond, beside some frog eggs. Days go by. Out wriggles a tadpole, the young.

k703.text: It grows legs, and its tail shrinks away. Out hops a frog. Egg, young, adult: three stages.

k704.text: Splash! You land in a flower-pot plate, beside tiny mosquito eggs. Out come the wrigglers, the larvae.

k705.text: Each one curls into a pupa, one more stage! Then out comes a mosquito. Egg, larva, pupa, adult: four stages.

k802.text: The answer is two: no, they are different! Two fingers? One finger up!

k803p.text: The frog has three stages, and the mosquito has four. The mosquito has a pupa, and the frog does not.

k804.text: Basil picked two, but size does not tell us about a life cycle. So only Pip scores a point.

k806.text: We can see the stages, and count them. They are observable characteristics.

k807p.text: Observable means we can see it, or count it. The number of stages is one. What the young looks like is another!

k902.text: The life cycles of the frog and the mosquito are similar because the young do not look like the adults. However, the life cycles are different because the frog has three stages in its life cycle, while the mosquito has four stages in its life cycle.

k1001p.text: My turn! The frog and the grasshopper both have three stages. So their life cycles are exactly the same!

k1002.text: Something is not right. If you can spot it, cross your arms. Hold on!

k1004b.text: The number of stages is the same, but you forgot to look at the young!

k1101.text: Look closer at the young, beside their parents.

k1102m.text: The tadpole has a tail and no legs, and it lives in water. It looks nothing like a frog!

k1103b.text: But the nymph has six legs and two feelers, just like a grasshopper. It only has no wings yet!

k1104.text: One thing is the same, and one thing is different. Always look at both!

k1107.text: When we compare, we can use observable characteristics to identify similarities and differences between the life cycles of the animals.

k1201.text: Show me your score hand! One finger or more? You beat the Buddies. Two fingers? High five!

k1202.text: Did you spot the cicada? It was on the leg of our board's easel!

k1203b.text: Here is a fun fact! Cicadas have three stages, like grasshoppers. But in America, some cicada nymphs live underground for seventeen years!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?

k1301b.text: Look, the hen is sitting on her eggs! So which came first, the chicken or the egg?
